question.text:
A portfolio manager is analyzing the performance of a mixed-asset portfolio consisting of 40% equities, 40% bonds, and 20% commodities. The expected return of equities is 10%, bonds is 5%, and commodities is 8%. The standard deviation of equities is 12%, bonds is 6%, and commodities is 10%. The risk-free rate is 3%. The correlations between the asset classes are as follows: equities and bonds: 0.2, equities and commodities: 0.4, bonds and commodities: 0.3.
Which asset class contributes the most to the portfolio's risk?

explanation.text: The Logic: Risk contribution depends on weight, individual standard deviation, and correlation with the other holdings. Equities combine the highest individual standard deviation (12%) with a 40% weight, making the equity sleeve the dominant driver of portfolio risk under the stated covariance inputs. The Trap: Bonds tempt candidates who give equal credit to the 40% weight without checking standard deviation. Commodities tempt those who notice the 10% SD but forget the small 20% weight. "All contribute equally" tempts those who assume equal weights mean equal risk contribution. Note: The reliance of portfolio risk on weights, standard deviations, and correlations is set out in the source workbook on the cited page.
